name: Caching Strategy Implementation
description: solution_code (Python) defines a Cache class driven, in order, through a harness-controlled operation sequence -- get / put / advance_time / check_store -- and its real hit/miss result, returned value, and evicted-key identity at every step must match that operation's curator-declared expected outcome. Ground truth is never trusted blindly: the harness FIRST independently recomputes, from cache_policy + policy_params alone (via its own reference implementation of the declared algorithm -- lru / lfu / fifo / ttl / write_through -- never by inspecting solution_code or trusting the row's own claims), what every operation's outcome must be, and rejects the row outright if the curator's own declared sequence does not match that independent computation. solution_code is mechanically forbidden from reading the real system clock: any TTL logic must decide purely from the `now` argument the harness passes into get()/put(), never a real sleep or a real clock read.
executionEnv: python3 (stdlib only). No real time.sleep()/time.time()/datetime.now() is ever used to drive this category's timing -- every 'second' in a row's operations sequence is a plain number the harness passes directly to solution_code's Cache.get(key, now)/Cache.put(key, value, now, ttl_seconds), so a sequence spanning simulated hours (via advance_time) still verifies in well under a second of real wall-clock time. Applies uniformly to every cache_policy, not only 'ttl'.

fields.label: Task description
fields.help: Natural-language description of the cached resource/scenario, e.g. 'an in-process cache in front of a slow product-lookup call' or 'a per-session token cache for a small API gateway'. This is scenario framing/flavor text for the contributor and human/LLM audit stages -- the harness's own pass/fail decision is driven entirely by cache_policy + policy_params + operations below, never parsed from this field.

fields.label: Cache policy
fields.help: Selects which of this harness's own independently-implemented reference algorithms (see policy_params' help text for each one's EXACT pinned semantics -- eviction tie-break rules included) is used both to CROSS-CHECK operations' own declared expected outcomes before solution_code ever runs, and to grade solution_code's real behavior against. write_back/read-through are deliberately NOT supported by this category -- write_back needs dirty-bit tracking and an explicit flush/invalidation contract that meaningfully complicates the operation vocabulary and oracle for a policy that is less commonly asked about than the other five; read-through is a related but distinct pattern from write_through (see solution_code's own help text) that this category does not test. fifo is included alongside the more commonly requested lru/lfu/ttl because it is nearly free to oracle-compute (a strict subset of lru's own bookkeeping, minus the touch-on-access rule) and is a genuinely distinct, well-known eviction discipline worth covering.

fields.label: Policy description
fields.help: Natural-language statement of the EXACT policy solution_code must implement, restating policy_params' own numbers in prose so a contributor reading only this field (not policy_params, which is curator-only ground truth never shown as 'the answer' -- see its own help text) knows precisely what to build, e.g. 'LRU cache, capacity 3: evict the least-recently-used key when a 4th distinct key is inserted', 'LFU cache, capacity 2, ties broken by least-recently-used', 'TTL cache, capacity 4, default 10-second TTL per entry, lazily expired (checked and purged on every get/put, never a background sweep)', 'write-through cache, capacity 2: every put synchronously persists to a separate backing store that survives cache eviction'. Must state the SAME numbers as policy_params -- the two fields are authored together by the curator, describing one policy from two angles (prose for the contributor to read and implement against; structured JSON for the harness's own oracle to compute against mechanically), the same convention rate_limiting_policy_simulation's policy_description/policy_params pair already established for this registry.

fields.label: Policy parameters (curator-authored ground truth, JSON)
fields.help: Curator-authored, fixed context (never graded, never written by the contributor, never sent into solution_code's own Python subprocess at all -- see harness.js's own module doc comment on why the oracle and solution_code run in fully separate address spaces). A JSON object: {"capacity": N} (a positive integer) for lru/lfu/fifo/write_through; {"capacity": N, "default_ttl_seconds": N} (both positive) for ttl. This is the ONLY input the harness's own independent reference-oracle computation trusts -- it is computed from cache_policy + policy_params alone, then cross-checked against every operation's own declared expected_result/expected_value/expected_evicted_key/expected_present in `operations` BEFORE solution_code is ever run; a row whose operations do not match what its own declared cache_policy/policy_params actually produce is rejected outright as a dataset-authoring defect. EXACT PINNED SEMANTICS PER cache_policy (author expected outcomes in `operations` by hand-applying these EXACT rules -- every rule below applies identically across all five policies unless stated otherwise): a capacity-triggered eviction happens ONLY when inserting a genuinely NEW key while the cache already holds `capacity` resident entries -- an update-put to an ALREADY-resident key never itself triggers eviction, regardless of policy. lru -- eviction removes the single least-recently-used resident key; 'used' means any get(hit) OR any put (insert or update) touching that key, which moves it to the most-recently-used end; no ties are possible (a single global recency order). lfu -- each resident key carries a frequency counter, incremented by 1 on every get(hit) AND every put (insert or update) touching it; a freshly-inserted key starts at frequency 1 (it has just been 'used' once, by being inserted); eviction removes the key with the SMALLEST frequency among resident keys, ties broken by LRU (the least-recently-used among the tied minimum-frequency keys is evicted). fifo -- eviction order is pure insertion order among resident keys, fixed the moment each key is FIRST inserted and never altered by any later get or update-put to that same key (an update-put changes only the stored value, never its position); eviction removes the single oldest-inserted resident key. ttl -- lazy expiration, purge-first: BEFORE evaluating any get or put, the cache first purges every resident entry whose own expiry has already passed (expiresAt <= now counts as expired -- a boundary tie is expired, mirroring rate_limiting_policy_simulation's own sliding_window_log boundary convention); a get for a key that was just purged (or was never present) is a miss; a put on an already-resident (post-purge) key is an update -- overwrites its value, resets its expiry to now + (this put's own ttl_seconds override if given, else the cache's own default_ttl_seconds), and refreshes its LRU recency; a put on a NOT-resident (post-purge) key is a genuine insert, subject to the same capacity-triggered LRU-tie-broken eviction rule as plain lru (evicted only if the cache is still at capacity AFTER the purge step -- so a merely-stale, not-yet-accessed entry is reclaimed by capacity pressure before a live one is ever evicted); the newly inserted entry's own expiry is now + its own ttl_seconds. write_through -- identical eviction semantics to lru (capacity, LRU-ordered, no ties), PLUS: every put (insert or update) synchronously writes (key, value) into a SEPARATE, permanent backing store that a capacity-triggered cache eviction never prunes (the backing store only ever grows/overwrites via put, exactly mirroring a real write-through cache's durability guarantee); get() consults ONLY the in-memory cache layer, never the backing store -- see solution_code's own help text for why read-through fallback is deliberately out of scope for this category. AUTHORING GUIDANCE: prefer clean integer/simple-decimal values (avoid values that only agree exactly under floating-point arithmetic) so hand-computed expected outcomes are unambiguous; keep capacity small relative to the number of distinct keys the operations sequence inserts, so a genuine eviction is actually forced (see operations' own anti-hardcoding gate, which mechanically rejects a sequence that never exercises one).

fields.label: Cache implementation (Python)
fields.help: THE GRADED ARTIFACT. Python code defining EXACTLY ONE top-level class named `Cache`, with a no-argument constructor (`def __init__(self):` -- hardcode this row's own policy_description/policy_params numbers inside it; the harness never passes policy parameters in) and these methods, with EXACTLY this signature shape (uniform across every cache_policy, so contributors of a non-time-based policy simply never use the `now`/`ttl_seconds` arguments -- they are still always passed): `def get(self, key, now):` returning a 2-tuple `(hit, value)` -- `(True, <the stored value>)` on a hit, `(False, None)` on a miss. A 2-tuple, not a bare value, deliberately: a bare 'return None means miss' convention cannot distinguish 'key absent' from 'key present with a genuinely stored value of JSON null', which this category's own `operations` field permits. `def put(self, key, value, now, ttl_seconds=None):` storing value under key and returning the STRING key that was evicted to make room, or None if no eviction occurred. A capacity-triggered eviction happens ONLY when inserting a genuinely NEW key while already at capacity -- an update to an EXISTING key's value must never itself evict anything. `ttl_seconds` is only ever meaningful for cache_policy 'ttl' (None means 'use this cache's own default_ttl_seconds'; a number overrides it for this one entry) -- other policies receive it as always-None and should ignore it. Additionally, ONLY for cache_policy 'write_through': `def get_from_store(self, key):` returning a 2-tuple `(present, value)` reflecting this cache's own SEPARATE, permanent backing store (a plain dict this class owns and mutates synchronously inside put() -- never a real external service/file/network call) -- present/value must reflect exactly what the most recent put() for that key wrote, REGARDLESS of whether that key has since been evicted from the in-memory cache (the backing store is the durable source of truth and is never pruned by cache eviction). CRITICAL, DELIBERATE SCOPE BOUNDARY for write_through: get() must consult ONLY the in-memory cache, NEVER the backing store -- this category tests write-through semantics (synchronous write propagation), not read-through semantics (falling back to a backing store on a cache miss and repopulating from it), a related but genuinely different pattern this category does not cover; a get() for an evicted key is a real cache miss even though get_from_store() for that same key still reports it present. CRITICAL, MECHANICALLY ENFORCED CONSTRAINT (every cache_policy alike, not only 'ttl'): Cache must decide every outcome using ONLY the `now` argument passed into get()/put() -- it must NEVER read the real system clock (no `time.time()`, `time.monotonic()`, `datetime.now()`/`.utcnow()`, or any other real-clock source) and must NEVER really sleep (`time.sleep()` is forbidden -- there is no reason to sleep at all: every 'second' in this category is a plain number, not something to wait for). Enforced two ways, identical to rate_limiting_policy_simulation's own proven mechanism: (1) a static check rejects solution_code outright if it contains a literal import of time/datetime/calendar or a call to any of their clock-reading functions; (2) as a mechanical backstop against any indirect/dynamic import that dodges (1), the harness replaces sys.modules['time']/['datetime']/['calendar'] with stub objects that raise immediately on ANY attribute access, before solution_code is ever executed.

fields.label: Operation sequence
fields.help: JSON array of at least 4 operations, executed IN ORDER against a single Cache() instance (mirroring one continuous, long-lived cache instance handling a real request stream over time), each one of four shapes: {"op": "get", "key": "<string>", "expected_result": "hit" | "miss", "expected_value": <required IFF expected_result is "hit" -- the exact JSON value curator-hand-computed to be resident under that key at this point, omitted/absent when "miss">}; {"op": "put", "key": "<string>", "value": <any JSON value>, "ttl_seconds": <optional positive number, cache_policy "ttl" ONLY -- overrides policy_params.default_ttl_seconds for this one entry>, "expected_evicted_key": <the STRING key curator-hand-computed to be evicted BY THIS PUT, or JSON null if this put must not evict anything -- REQUIRED on every put, the PRIMARY, direct eviction-correctness check this category relies on (see harness.js's own module doc comment for why an explicit field is preferred here over inferring eviction identity purely from later get results, which this schema's own authoring guidance below still separately encourages as a secondary, natural confirmation)>}; {"op": "advance_time", "seconds": <positive number>} -- cache_policy "ttl" ONLY, advances the harness's own virtual clock (starts at 0) by this many seconds for every SUBSEQUENT get/put's own `now` argument; {"op": "check_store", "key": "<string>", "expected_present": true | false, "expected_value": <required IFF expected_present is true>} -- cache_policy "write_through" ONLY, inspects the backing store directly (bypassing the cache layer) via Cache.get_from_store(). Every expected_* value MUST be curator-computed by hand-applying cache_policy/policy_params' own EXACT pinned semantics (see policy_params' help text) -- never guessed. Independently double-checked by the harness's own reference-oracle computation before solution_code ever runs -- an operations/policy pairing that is self-consistent but does not actually match what the declared policy produces is rejected as a dataset-authoring defect, not silently accepted. ANTI-HARDCODING, MECHANICALLY ENFORCED (four separate gates -- see harness.js's own module doc comment for the full reasoning behind each): (1) not every `get`'s expected_result may be identical (author at least one genuine hit AND one genuine miss); (2) at least one `put` must declare a non-null expected_evicted_key -- author enough distinct-key puts to genuinely exceed policy_params.capacity at least once; (3) for cache_policy "ttl", at least one `advance_time` must appear -- a TTL row that never advances the virtual clock cannot prove expiry is real; (4) for cache_policy "write_through", at least one `check_store` must appear -- a row that never inspects the backing store cannot prove write-through persistence is real. AUTHORING GUIDANCE for the strongest rows (encouraged, not mechanically required beyond the four gates above): after a put that evicts key K, follow up with a later `get` for K expecting "miss" (confirms eviction from the cache's own read path, not merely from Cache.put's own self-reported return value) and a `get` for a key that should have SURVIVED that same eviction expecting "hit" with its correct value (confirms the SURVIVOR was chosen correctly, not merely that SOME eviction happened); for write_through rows, author a `check_store` for a key AFTER it has been evicted from the cache (expected_present true) to prove the backing store genuinely outlives cache eviction, not merely that it was written once.
